proposalTitle: Searching the Kubernetes Scheduler Policy Space: Lessons From Noisy Live Optimization
presentationTitleAlternative: When the Optimizer Learns the Noise: Lessons From Live Kubernetes Scheduler Tuning
coreClaim: Under equal live-evaluation budgets, two-stage resampling produced fewer false Pareto discoveries than one-shot search among three finalists per arm, but holdout validation showed that the remaining apparent gain was a baseline near-tie rather than robust scheduler superiority.
claimBoundaries: Do not claim that evolutionary search found a scheduler superior to the default Kubernetes scheduler.
Call one-shot fronts provisional and repeated-mean fronts point-estimate Pareto fronts.
Do not treat overlapping latency confidence intervals as statistically distinct.
Treat the 2/3 versus 1/3 false-discovery comparison as descriptive because each arm contributes only three finalists.
Describe the mixed-burst holdout as unseen to V3 selection, not fully blinded, because its earlier V2 baseline outcomes were known.
Describe maximum workload-occupied workers as a consolidation proxy, not powered-node cost.
Describe kind as a reproducible testbed, not production-scale evidence.

slides.title: We found a better policy. Then we repeated the experiment.
slides.purpose: Open with the methodological reversal, not an evolutionary-computation tutorial.
slides.visual: One sentence and the 5-to-0 transition from the killer figure.
slides.speakerPoint: The optimizer result looked convincing across three seeds, but shared repeated validation changed the conclusion.

slides.title: The scheduling tradeoff
slides.purpose: Define the two objectives and their limits.
slides.visual: Latency versus workload-occupied workers with a small Pareto sketch.
slides.speakerPoint: We minimize p95 scheduler-decision latency and a consolidation proxy without collapsing them into one score.

slides.title: A live Kubernetes evaluation loop
slides.purpose: Establish that candidates cause real rollouts and Pod bindings.
slides.visual: System architecture: optimizer, evaluator, scheduler deployment, kind workers, and artifacts.
slides.speakerPoint: Each candidate patches the scheduler, waits for convergence, replays three workloads, and records high-resolution decisions.

slides.title: The first policy space was not identifiable
slides.purpose: Show the scale-equivalence and redundant-packing failure without hiding it.
slides.visual: V1 score reduction followed by the normalized V2 simplex.
slides.speakerPoint: Different chromosomes could express equivalent rankings, so we normalized weights and separated balance from consolidation.

slides.title: Measure the decision, not the observer
slides.purpose: Separate scheduler decision time, Kubernetes timestamps, and evaluator observation lag.
slides.visual: A timing line with submission, scheduler decision, PodScheduled, and evaluator observation.
slides.speakerPoint: Feasibility stays fixed; decision timestamps come from the scheduler, and incomplete or protocol-drifted evaluations are rejected.

slides.title: The first win disappeared under repetition
slides.purpose: Use V2 as the falsifiable motivation for noise-aware search.
slides.visual: The V2 one-shot-to-repeated-validation collapse figure: five selected finalists to zero survivors.
slides.speakerPoint: Three seeds looked convincing, but none of five finalists remained nondominated when every policy-workload pair was repeated ten times.

slides.title: Can resampling help without buying more cluster time?
slides.purpose: State the V3 mitigation question and its equal-budget constraint.
slides.visual: Budget diagram: 72 one-shot candidates versus 42 candidates plus 30 promotion samples per arm and seed.
slides.speakerPoint: Both arms receive 72 fresh samples per seed; two-stage search trades exploration breadth for repeated estimates of promoted candidates.

slides.title: Same budget, fewer observed false discoveries
slides.purpose: Present the shared-validation result without turning a small denominator into inference.
slides.visual: Left panel of the V3 killer figure: one-shot 2/3 and two-stage 1/3 false Pareto discoveries.
slides.speakerPoint: Two-stage produced fewer observed failures among three finalists per arm, a directional result rather than statistical proof.

slides.title: Holdout turns the survivor into a near-tie
slides.purpose: Show why promotion still requires held-out evidence.
slides.visual: Right panel of the V3 killer figure with six policies, confidence intervals, and the 43-microsecond annotation.
slides.speakerPoint: Only one of three survivors remains nondominated, and it differs from consolidation by 43 microseconds at the same mean worker count with overlapping intervals.

slides.title: A checklist for noisy live optimization
slides.purpose: Convert the study into reusable practitioner guidance.
slides.visual: Seven checks: identifiable policy, timestamp provenance, equal budgets, hard validity gates, repeated promotion, held-out validation, immutable artifacts.
slides.speakerPoint: Replication must be budgeted into search and promotion, not added only after an attractive result appears.

slides.title: Questions
slides.visual: Repository and paper links only after they are anonymously accessible.
slides.speakerPoint: Invite questions about scheduler design, live measurement, Pareto interpretation, and noise-aware search.

segments.script: What happens when an optimizer reports a better Kubernetes scheduling policy? The tempting answer is that it found a smarter scheduler. That was also my first result. Then I repeated every finalist, and all five apparent improvements disappeared. The next question was harder: can we reduce these false discoveries without buying more cluster time?

I built a custom Kubernetes scheduler with four normalized policy weights. An NSGA-II-style optimizer generated candidates, and an evaluator patched each policy into a running deployment on a four-worker kind cluster. Every sample caused real rollouts, three 24-Pod workload replays, and real Pod bindings. We measured p95 scheduler-decision latency and the maximum workers occupied by the workload.

The initial three-seed search evaluated 216 candidates once per workload and produced five optimizer-only provisional Pareto points. If I had stopped there, the conclusion would have been that evolutionary search found better tradeoffs. Instead, I ran each finalist and baseline ten times on every training workload. None of the five optimizer finalists remained nondominated. The optimizer had found timing luck, not a robust policy improvement.

For the follow-up, I fixed the live-evaluation budget. In each seed, one-shot search spent 72 samples on 72 candidates. Two-stage search evaluated 42 candidates and spent the remaining 30 samples re-evaluating promoted policies. Across seeds 42, 123, and 999, each arm consumed 216 optimizer samples. Together they executed 1,350 workload replays and 32,400 Pods without an unschedulable result.

Shared validation then measured three finalists from each arm ten times on each workload. Two of three one-shot finalists were false Pareto discoveries, compared with one of three two-stage finalists. That direction is encouraging, but three finalists per arm are too few for a statistical claim. The result says that resampling helped in this frozen experiment, not that it is universally better.

The fixed holdout was stricter. Only one of the three validation survivors remained nondominated. At the same mean 2.1 occupied workers, its p95 latency differed from the hand-designed consolidation policy by only 43 microseconds, with strongly overlapping intervals. Exact Pareto arithmetic kept the point; practical evidence did not support a superiority claim.

segments.onScreen: Speaker on camera with seven-item checklist
segments.script: The lesson is broader than scheduling. Make the policy identifiable, know where every timestamp comes from, compare methods under equal budgets, reject invalid samples, repeat before promotion, validate on held-out workloads, and preserve raw evidence. Otherwise, an optimizer can learn measurement noise as efficiently as it learns the system. That is the experiment and practical playbook I want to share at KubeCon Europe.
